lc-coenobita-clypeatus.title: Caribbean Hermit Crab (Purple Pincher)
lc-coenobita-clypeatus.summary: The common pet land hermit crab of the western Atlantic, named for its big purple left claw. It breathes air with modified gills, so it needs warm, humid air, deep moist sand to molt in, fresh and salt water, and a supply of spare shells. With good care it lives for many years.
rows: Adults can reach 8–10 cm in leg reach; size varies a lot
Glass or plastic tank with a secure lid; about 10 gal per small to medium crab as a starting point, more for big crabs or groups. Add climbing branches, hides and leaf litter
At least 6 in of moist, burrowable sand/coconut-fiber mix (or 3× the height of the largest crab) so crabs can bury themselves to molt
About 75–85°F with a gentle warm-to-cool gradient
About 70–85%; low humidity damages their modified gills
Two pools deep enough to submerge in but easy to climb out of: dechlorinated fresh water and salt water made with marine aquarium salt

Varied omnivore and scavenger: fruit (e.g. coconut, mango, apple), leafy greens, dried oak leaves, nuts, protein (dried shrimp, fish, egg) and calcium such as cuttlebone. No foods with preservatives, table salt or copper
Social: keep with compatible companions and duplicate food, water and shells to cut competition
Nocturnal; climbs, digs and explores at night
Caribbean, southern Florida, Belize and northern South America (coastal forest and scrub)
notes: Always offer several spare natural, unpainted shells near the current size and slightly larger. Painted shells can chip and trap the crab.
Crabs molt buried in the substrate for days to weeks; never dig one up.

lc-coenobita-compressus.title: Ecuadorian Hermit Crab
lc-coenobita-compressus.summary: A small, fast, Pacific-coast land hermit crab and the other species commonly sold as a pet in North America besides the Caribbean hermit crab. It has oval eyes and needs the same warm, humid setup with deep sand, fresh and salt water and spare shells.

lc-coenobita-perlatus.title: Strawberry Hermit Crab
lc-coenobita-perlatus.summary: A bright red-orange land hermit crab from islands across the Indo-Pacific. Like all land hermit crabs it isn't an easy pet: it needs warm, humid air, deep moist sand, fresh and salt water and plenty of spare shells.
rows: Typically about 80 mm (3 in) long and about 80 g
Glass or plastic tank with a secure lid; about 10 gal per small to medium crab as a starting point, more for big crabs or groups. Add climbing branches, hides and leaf litter
At least 6 in of moist, burrowable sand/coconut-fiber mix (or 3× the height of the largest crab) so crabs can bury themselves to molt
About 75–85°F with a gentle warm-to-cool gradient
About 70–85%; low humidity damages their modified gills
Two pools deep enough to submerge in but easy to climb out of: dechlorinated fresh water and salt water made with marine aquarium salt
Scavenging omnivore: fruit, vegetables, protein and a calcium source
Social: keep with compatible companions and duplicate food, water and shells to cut competition
Indo-Pacific islands, from Indonesia, Mauritius and the Seychelles east to Samoa
notes: Always offer several spare natural, unpainted shells near the current size and slightly larger. Painted shells can chip and trap the crab.
Crabs molt buried in the substrate for days to weeks; never dig one up.

lc-coenobita-purpureus.title: Blueberry Hermit Crab
lc-coenobita-purpureus.summary: A blue-to-purple land hermit crab from islands in the North Pacific, including southern Japan. Nearly all are wild-caught because they are very hard to breed. Care is the same warm, humid, deep-sand setup as other land hermit crabs.
rows: About 7–10 cm long (shell opening about 3–4 cm)
Glass or plastic tank with a secure lid; about 10 gal per small to medium crab as a starting point, more for big crabs or groups. Add climbing branches, hides and leaf litter
At least 6 in of moist, burrowable sand/coconut-fiber mix (or 3× the height of the largest crab) so crabs can bury themselves to molt
About 75–85°F with a gentle warm-to-cool gradient
About 70–85%; low humidity damages their modified gills
Two pools deep enough to submerge in but easy to climb out of: dechlorinated fresh water and salt water made with marine aquarium salt
Omnivorous scavenger: fruit, vegetables, protein and a calcium source
Social: keep with compatible companions and duplicate food, water and shells to cut competition
North Pacific islands, including the Ryukyu Islands (Okinawa) and parts of Japan
notes: Always offer several spare natural, unpainted shells near the current size and slightly larger. Painted shells can chip and trap the crab.
Crabs molt buried in the substrate for days to weeks; never dig one up.
